title: Letter I
focus: ambition and the hunger for discovery

teacherSummary.text: Robert Walton writes to his sister Margaret Saville from St. Petersburg. He is about to sail toward the North Pole, eager to discover a passage and the secret of the magnet, and he describes his self-education and longing for glory.

vocabulary.definition: The act or practice of alluring or tempting
vocabulary.context: My life might have been passed in ease and luxury; but I preferred glory to every enticement that wealth placed in my path.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “enticement”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into") + -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: My courage and my resolution is firm; but my hopes fluctuate, and my spirits are often depressed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fluctuate”: luc (Latin lux, "light") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: These visions faded when I perused, for the first time, those poets whose effusions entranced my soul, and lifted it to heaven.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “effusion”: -sion (Latin -sio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I shall satiate my ardent curiosity with the sight of a part of the world never before visited, and may tread a land never before imprinted by the foot of man.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “satiate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: This breeze, which has travelled from the regions towards which I am advancing, gives me a foretaste of those icy climes.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “foretaste”: fore- (Old English fore, "before"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of entering or going into
vocabulary.context: These visions faded when I perused, for the first time, those poets whose effusions entranced my soul, and lifted it to heaven.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “entrance”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To pour out and cause to spread, as a fluid
vocabulary.context: There, Margaret, the sun is forever visible; its broad disk just skirting the horizon, and diffusing a perpetual splendour.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “diffuse”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A strong vehicle with low runners or low wheels
vocabulary.context: They fly quickly over the snow in their sledges; the motion is pleasant, and, in my opinion, far more agreeable than that of an English stagecoach.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sledge”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Following the business of a mariner
vocabulary.context: These volumes were my study day and night, and my familiarity with them increased that regret which I had felt, as a child, on learning that my father’s dying injunction had forbidden my uncle to allow me to embark in a seafaring life.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “seafaring”: se- (Latin se-, "apart") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “foreboding”: fore- (Old English fore, "before") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Arctic exploration and the search for a Northwest Passage were major public dreams in the early 1800s. Letters were a popular novel form (the epistolary novel).

significance: Walton is Victor's double: an ambitious man willing to risk others for discovery. The frame narrative invites readers to judge whether he will learn from Victor.
discussionQuestions: What do Walton's dreams of the North Pole reveal about his character?
Where does point of view appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with isolation and the need for companionship?

items.prompt: Where is Walton when he writes the first letter?
What does Walton hope to discover?
options: A passage near the pole and the secret of the magnet

items.prompt: How did Walton educate himself as a boy?
options: Reading his uncle's library of voyages
Victor's own dangerous pursuit of knowledge

items.prompt: In the line “My life might have been passed in ease and luxury; but I preferred glory to every enticement that wealth placed in my path.”, what does “enticement” most nearly mean?
options: The act or practice of alluring or tempting

items.prompt: In the line “My courage and my resolution is firm; but my hopes fluctuate, and my spirits are often depressed.”, what does “fluctuate” most nearly mean?
options: The act or practice of alluring or tempting

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Letter I,” how does Shelley show ambition and the hunger for discovery? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Letter I develops the idea of ambition and the hunger for discovery. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses point of view in Letter I to complicate the reader's understanding of ambition and the hunger for discovery. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Letter I within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of ambition and the hunger for discovery responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Letter I as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of ambition and the hunger for discovery. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Letter I”?

The first death and growing guilt
Ambition and the hunger for discovery

annotationFocus.label: Point of view
annotationFocus.lookFor: who is telling the story and what that narrator can and cannot know
annotationFocus.passage: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings. I arrived here yesterday; and my first task is to assure my dear sister of my welfare, and increasing confidence in the success of my undertaking.

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing

annotationFocus.label: Characterization

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What do Walton's dreams of the North Pole reveal about his character? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are enticement, fluctuate, effusions, satiate, foretaste. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “My life might have been passed in ease and luxury; but I preferred glory to every enticement that wealth placed in my path.” Webster's says: The act or practice of alluring or tempting. Now the word history: “enticement”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into") + -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “fluctuate”: luc (Latin lux, "light") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “effusion”: -sion (Latin -sio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Arctic exploration and the search for a Northwest Passage were major public dreams in the early 1800s. Letters were a popular novel form (the epistolary novel). Why does this chapter matter? Walton is Victor's double: an ambitious man willing to risk others for discovery. The frame narrative invites readers to judge whether he will learn from Victor. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see point of view, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to ambition and the hunger for discovery.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Point of view, Foreshadowing, Characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings. I arrived here yesterday; and my first task is to assure my dear sister of my welfare, and increasing confidence in the success of my undertaking.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Point of view, Foreshadowing, Characterization: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Letter I,” how does Shelley show ambition and the hunger for discovery? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about ambition and the hunger for discovery, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how point of view shapes ambition and the hunger for discovery. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
